Description: 4Q51, also called 4QSama, is the most extensive Samuel manuscript from Qumran, written in Hebrew in the Herodian period (about 50-25 BC). Hundreds of fragments survive from what was originally a scroll of some 55-60 columns, spanning 1 Samuel 1 through 2 Samuel 24. It was found in Qumran Cave 4 in 1952. Its readings often agree with the ancient Greek Septuagint against the later Masoretic Text.
Interpretations: The scroll's most famous contribution is a longer passage before 1 Samuel 11:1 describing Nahash's oppression of the Gadites and Reubenites, gouging out their right eyes, with 7,000 escaping to Jabesh-Gilead; this explains the sudden opening of chapter 11 and was adopted by modern translations such as the NRSV. Whether that passage is original or a secondary expansion is debated: Frank Moore Cross and Emanuel Tov accept it as original, while Dominique Barthelemy and others view it as an expansion, a stalemate noted in recent scholarship. Either way, the scroll shows that more than one Hebrew form of Samuel circulated in the Second Temple period.
BiblicalSignificance: It supplies the missing background to 1 Samuel 11 and proves that the Hebrew text of Samuel existed in more than one ancient form, sometimes agreeing with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text.
